The Greenstriped rockfish (Sebastes elongatus) is a viviparous scorpaenid that inhabits the continental slope and outer shelf waters of the northeastern Pacific Ocean. Females of this species release live, free-swimming larvae following an extended gestation, rather than spawning pelagic eggs. At the onset of parturition, each newly extruded larva weighs approximately 0.000268 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.000268 grams], a value derived from the diameter of the developing ova within the ovary prior to fertilisation. This minute neonatal mass reflects the energetic constraints of producing large numbers of offspring from a single batch. Adult females that have completed their somatic growth can attain a maximum wet weight of 761 grams [Wwi = 761 grams], a substantial increase from the larval stage. This ultimate body mass is typically reached in individuals that have achieved the species’ asymptotic total length of 38 centimeters [Li = 38 centimeters]. Such large adults are relatively uncommon in trawl surveys, as size-selective fishing pressure tends to remove the oldest and largest individuals from the population before they reach their full growth potential.

Reproductive development in Sebastes elongatus follows a well-defined pattern linked to body size rather than age alone. The onset of puberty, marked by the first appearance of vitellogenic oocytes in the ovary, occurs when individuals reach a total length of approximately 18 centimeters [Lp = approximately 18 centimeters]. At this length, females typically weigh about 75.6 grams [Wwp = about 75.6 grams], a threshold that indicates they have redirected energy from somatic growth toward gametogenesis. This length at puberty is considerably smaller than the ultimate body size, suggesting that the species invests in an extended period of juvenile growth before initiating reproductive activity. Field studies off the coast of British Columbia have confirmed that most individuals have commenced gonadal recrudescence by the time they surpass this size threshold. The consistency of this pattern across different latitudinal ranges suggests a strong genetic basis for the timing of maturation onset.

The maximum reproductive output of this species has been quantified under controlled laboratory conditions that mimic the cold, stable thermal regime of its deepwater habitat. When maintained at a constant temperature of 7 °C [T = 7 °C], each spawning event yields approximately 344,000 larvae per event [N_R_i = approximately 344,000 larvae per event], corresponding to a maximum daily reproduction rate of approximately 942 larvae per day [Ri = approximately 942 larvae per day]. Such spawning occurs once per year [F_R_i = spawning occurs once per year]. This annual larval production is among the highest recorded within the genus Sebastes, consistent with the species’ strategy of producing a single, large brood each year. The high fecundity is likely an adaptation to the low survival probabilities experienced by the planktonic larval stage, where predation and advection away from suitable settlement habitat impose heavy mortality. The thermal regime is critical, as metabolic rates and the rate of yolk absorption in the developing embryos are directly influenced by ambient water temperature.

Longevity and metabolic performance in Sebastes elongatus are strongly shaped by the cold temperatures of its preferred depth range. Field mark-recapture studies and otolith age determination indicate that this species exhibits a maximum lifespan of approximately 54 years [am = approximately 54 years] under natural conditions, with the oldest verified individuals collected from waters maintained at 7 °C [T = 7 °C]. This remarkable longevity is characteristic of many rockfish species, which exhibit slow growth rates and delayed senescence as a consequence of their deepwater, low-metabolism lifestyle. The low ambient temperature is thought to decouple the accumulation of cellular damage from chronological time, thereby extending the functional lifespan. This extended life history strategy allows individuals to reproduce over many consecutive spawning seasons, potentially compensating for low recruitment in any single year.

Comparisons among congeners highlight the intermediate life-history strategy of Sebastes elongatus relative to other northeastern Pacific rockfishes. While the shortraker rockfish (Sebastes borealis) can exceed 120 years of age and attain much larger body sizes, the Greenstriped rockfish exhibits a more modest ultimate total length of 38 centimeters [Li = 38 centimeters]. Its maximum wet weight of 761 grams [Wwi = 761 grams] is also considerably lower than that of the larger-bodied slope species. However, both species share the trait of extreme longevity, with the Greenstriped rockfish regularly living for over five decades (54 years) [am = 54 years] at a temperature of 7 °C [T = 7 °C]. The age at first reproduction in this species, which typically occurs several years after the attainment of puberty at 18 centimeters [Lp = 18 centimeters] total length, ensures that most individuals have reached a body mass of at least 75.6 grams [Wwp = 75.6 grams] before producing their first brood. This conservative maturation schedule buffers the population against years of poor recruitment.
